drugRefs.dose: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h + Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
drugRefs.duration: Until cholecystectomy, or 4-7 days if surgery delayed/not performed
drugRefs.why: Covers the typical gram-negative and anaerobic biliary pathogens; definitive treatment is cholecystectomy, with antibiotics primarily bridging to surgery or covering milder cases managed non-operatively.

drugRefs.coverage: Broader single-agent option for more severe (Tokyo Guidelines grade II-III) cholecystitis.

coverageMatrix.completeness: Either regimen covers the major expected pathogens for typical acute cholecystitis.
gaps: Enterococcus not covered by ceftriaxone-based regimen — relevant mainly in severe/healthcare-associated cases.

stewardship.deescalation: If cholecystectomy is performed, antibiotics are often stopped within 24 hours post-operatively for uncomplicated cases (per Tokyo Guidelines); if managed non-operatively, narrow based on culture data and limit total duration.

drugs.dose: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h + Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
drugs.duration: Until cholecystectomy, or 4-7 days if surgery delayed/not performed
drugs.why: Covers the typical gram-negative and anaerobic biliary pathogens; definitive treatment is cholecystectomy, with antibiotics primarily bridging to surgery or covering milder cases managed non-operatively.

drugs.coverage: Broader single-agent option for more severe (Tokyo Guidelines grade II-III) cholecystitis.

framework: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 24-72 hours in eligible patients) is the definitive treatment — antibiotics are adjunctive, not a substitute for source control.
If surgery is delayed or the patient is not a surgical candidate, antibiotics can usually be limited to a defined short course rather than continued indefinitely.
Percutaneous cholecystostomy is an alternative source control measure in high-risk surgical candidates — antibiotics alone without some form of source control are often inadequate.
